whatShame.title: What shame is, and what guilt is
whatShame.lead: Guilt says "I did something bad". Shame says "I am bad". The whole path begins with this difference.
body: Guilt is about an act: a concrete thing you can name, repair or apologise for. It pulls towards action. Shame is about the whole self: "that's what I'm like", "something is wrong with me". It pulls towards hiding, disappearing, going silent. Tangney and Dearing's research shows guilt-proneness goes with empathy and repairing relationships, shame-proneness with depression, anxiety and anger.

In practice both often come together: a small act and a large "I'm hopeless". That's why the path asks every week "what is this shame about?" and separates three things: a deed (repair), an event that happened to you (care for yourself) and a demand that may not be yours (check it).
The point is not to stop feeling shame. The point is to recognise it sooner and know what to do with it, instead of letting it steer.
sources: Lewis 1971; Tangney & Dearing 2002; Kim, Thibodeau & Jorgensen 2011

notYourFault.title: Where shame comes from (not your fault)
notYourFault.lead: Shame is an alarm of the social threat system. Nobody chose their brain or their history.
body: Humans survived as a species thanks to the group. Losing acceptance used to be a real danger, so the brain has a built-in alarm that goes off when we feel we're losing our place among others. That alarm is shame. It fires fast, before we can think, and sets off old strategies: hide, attack yourself, attack others, look away.

Compassion-focused therapy calls this the "tricky brain": the system we were given and the history that tuned it are not our fault. What we do with it next is our business. Self-compassion isn't a reward for good behaviour. It's a muscle you train, as with a physiotherapist.
That's why the path starts with recognising and with the body, not with correcting thoughts. The alarm has to settle a little first; only then can another voice be heard.

compassParts.title: Four parts that take the wheel
compassParts.lead: The Hider, the Critic, the Accuser and the Avoider. Each protects. None of them is you.
body: Donald Nathanson described four automatic reactions to shame: withdrawal, attacking yourself, attacking others and avoidance. In parts language (IFS) each is a protector: a part that once learned to shield you from the pain of being seen. The Hider doesn't want you seen. The Critic gets ahead of other people's criticism so it hurts less. The Accuser pushes others away before the feeling of smallness can hurt. The Avoider moves the feeling itself out of the way.

Once the reaction has a name it stops being "that's what I'm like" and becomes "my part took the wheel". Someone in you is left who can hear it out and stay. That's what the unblending sentence in your shame response teaches, and every entry in Moments.

Honestly: IFS is a frame here for understanding and talking with yourself. The evidence for the path's effectiveness comes mainly from compassion-focused therapy, the Mindful Self-Compassion programme and chairwork.

threeSystems.title: Three emotion systems
threeSystems.lead: Threat, drive, soothing. Shame sits in the first. Warmth towards yourself needs the third.
body: The compassion-focused therapy model describes three emotion-regulation systems. The threat system looks for danger and responds with fear, anger, shame. The drive system chases reward and achievement. The soothing system handles calm, safety and connection; closeness, a warm voice, touch and a slow exhale switch it on.

In people with strong self-criticism the soothing system is often hard to reach: warmth towards yourself feels foreign, sometimes frightening. That's why in this path the soothing breath, the safe place and the compassionate image come before thinking. You can't argue the threat system down. You can settle it with the body, and only then speak.
A longer exhale than inhale, a hand on the heart, a calm tone of voice towards yourself: these aren't decorations of the exercises, they're the switch between systems.
sources: Gilbert 2009; Matos et al. 2017; Petrocchi, Ottaviani & Couyoumdjian 2017

whenWarmthHurts.title: When warmth hurts
whenWarmthHurts.lead: If sadness, anger or emptiness follows kindness to yourself, that's not a mistake. It's a door opening.
body: Chris Germer calls it "backdraft": let air into a closed, hot room and the fire flares. Let kindness into yourself and sometimes old pain flares: "where was this when I needed it?" It comes as tears, irritability, the thought "this isn't for me", pain in the body or the urge to abandon the exercise.

It's normal and common. It doesn't mean you're doing something wrong; it means the exercise reached where it was meant to. The rule: always practise at a level you can bear. If it's too much, close for today: return to the breath, to the safe place, to an ordinary activity that does you good. Every inward practice has a "Too much for today" button. Using it counts as practice too.

Resistance has its words too: "it's weakness", "I don't deserve it", "I'll get lazy", "I'll become dependent on it". Each of these voices protects against something. It's worth naming them rather than fighting them. If the pain after exercises doesn't pass or grows, see the card "When it's too much for self-help".
sources: Germer & Neff 2019; Gilbert, McEwan, Matos & Rivis 2011

actEventDemand.title: Deed, event, demand
actEventDemand.lead: Three answers to "what is this shame about?" and three ways forward: repair, care, check.
body: A deed: there was a real breach and it can be repaired. I forgot to call back, I criticised someone in front of people. Shame may be glued on ("I let the people close to me down"), but the core is the deed, so repair closes it. An event: there's no deed to repair. Failure, rejection, loss, illness. The answer is caring for yourself like a friend this happened to.

A demand: shame is guarding a rule that may not be yours or isn't fair. "Men don't cry at work", "after all these years I should know this". The test is simple: would you hold someone you like to this demand, and would you say they should be ashamed of it? If not, it's someone else's demand. The answer: check whose it is, phrase a fair one and do one thing against the unfair one.
Dialectical behaviour therapy calls the same thing checking the facts: justified shame leads to repair, unjustified shame to opposite action, which means not hiding.

readingProgress.title: How to read your progress
readingProgress.lead: More entries at the start is good. There are no streaks here. A week without moments is a quiet week, not a gap.
body: Progress on this path shows in three pictures from Moments. The first shows which part took the wheel week by week. At the start the bars grow because you start noticing; that's progress, not deterioration. Later what counts is how often no part took the wheel for good.

The second picture is the share of moments where you did anything instead of the reaction: a breath, naming, a sentence, contact. Every attempt counts, even an hour late. That fraction should grow slowly. The third picture is "when I notice": the share of moments noticed as they happened or shortly after. When it grows, the response has a chance to work.

The scale measures (SCS-SF and FSCRS) show the direction of change over time, not a verdict. The effects of such programmes are often delayed: in studies the difference often appeared only after two months. That's why the path comes back to you eight weeks after it ends.
sources: Neff & Germer 2013; Halamová et al. 2018; Breines & Chen 2012

criticProtector.title: The critic protects (and how to thank it)
criticProtector.lead: We don't silence the critic. We change the method it uses.
body: Self-criticism has two functions: correcting ("keep your standards, improve") and persecuting ("you deserve punishment"). People hold on to the critic because they believe it motivates and protects against others' criticism. Research says otherwise: after failure, kindness to yourself increases the wish to improve, and attack kills it. In compassion training groups the correcting function stays; only shame as its fuel goes.

Paul Gilbert compares it to two teachers. One points out the mistake with encouragement, looks forward, speaks about the specific behaviour, builds on what went well. The other condemns, looks back, speaks about all of you, threatens. Both want you to improve. Only the first one works.

That's why in week five you ask the critic: what are you afraid would happen if you stopped? Usually the answer is: that they'll reject you. That concern can be respected. The method can be changed. The sentence "thank you for keeping watch, I'm driving now" does exactly that.
sources: Gilbert, Clarke, Hempel, Miles & Irons 2004; Gilbert & Procter 2006; Breines & Chen 2012

notIndulgence.title: Compassion is not indulgence
notIndulgence.lead: The most common resistance: "I'll get lazy". The data say the opposite. And compassion has a fierce side too.
body: In Breines and Chen's experiments, people who treated themselves with compassion after a failure studied longer and were more willing to repair mistakes than those who shored up their self-esteem or distracted themselves. Compassion doesn't lower standards. It removes the fear that keeps you from approaching them.

Kristin Neff describes two sides of compassion. The tender one comforts, validates, keeps company. The fierce one protects, sets boundaries, says "enough", motivates. For someone who hears a voice of contempt inside, warmth alone is often not enough. They also need someone who will take their side. That's what the "Defending voice" exercise and the tasks teach: one "no" without explanation, head up, a sentence without "sorry".
Self-compassion isn't excusing yourself. It's what lets you look at your own mistake without running from it.

outOfHiding.title: Out of hiding
outOfHiding.lead: Shame says disappear. Being seen by someone kind heals it.
body: Shame lives in hiding. Every time you hide, it confirms there was something to be ashamed of. That's why the last weeks of the path are small exposures to being seen: stay a minute longer, ask a "stupid" question, show unfinished work, tell one safe person about something you're ashamed of.

Dialectical behaviour therapy calls this opposite action: when shame doesn't fit the facts, do the opposite of what it says. Instead of lowering your eyes, lift them. Instead of softening your voice, speak fully. Instead of hiding, say it. Brené Brown calls the last move "speaking shame" and points out that another person's empathy is what disarms shame most effectively.

The behavioural experiment in week seven tests a concrete prediction: "if they see the real me, they'll reject me". A small, safe situation, the prediction written down, then the result. Usually the gap between what you expect and what happens teaches more than a week of talking to yourself.
sources: Rizvi & Linehan 2005; Brown 2006; Bennett-Levy et al. 2004

whenTooMuch.title: When it's too much for self-help
whenTooMuch.lead: This path helps with ordinary shame. Some things need a person, not an app.
body: Some signals mean it's worth pausing the path and talking to a professional: shame tied to violence, abuse or another serious injury; memories that return against your will, with a loss of contact with the here and now; thoughts of hurting yourself or a sense that you deserve punishment; pain after exercises that doesn't pass but grows; long weeks without energy, sleep or joy.

That's not a failure of the path or of you. Compassion programmes are effective and safe for most people, but in studies the most deeply ashamed most often dropped out on their own because the programme "looked disappointed". There's none of that here: you can pause the path, come back to it in a month or start over.
If you need to talk now, in Poland the 24-hour crisis helpline for adults is 116 123. In an immediate threat to life, call 112.
sources: Saraiya & Lopez-Castro 2016; Northover et al. 2021; Cai 2024
